text: It is hard to get direct evidence of prospective reasoning in animals. <break time="0.8s" /> But there is now good behavioral evidence of capacities. <break time="0.8s" /> That, in humans. <break time="0.8s" /> Would be enabled by prospection. <break time="0.8s" /> Most of this work has been done. <break time="0.8s" /> With corvids and with great apes. <break time="0.8s" /> For instance. <break time="0.8s" /> Animals from both groups. <break time="0.8s" /> Can solve the floating peanut problem. <break time="0.8s" /> Seemingly by insight. <break time="0.8s" /> Rather than trial and error. <break time="0.8s" /> This is the problem. <break time="0.8s" /> Of how to reach a food item. <break time="0.8s" /> That is too far down in a clear, fixed tube. <break time="0.8s" /> To be reached by hand or beak. <break time="0.8s" /> The solution is to spit water into the tube. <break time="0.8s" /> In the case of the chimps. <break time="0.8s" /> Or to drop stones into the tube that already contains some water. <break time="0.8s" /> In the case of the rooks. <break time="0.8s" /> So as to float the item far enough up. <break time="0.8s" /> To be reached. <break time="0.8s" /> The same problem is solved. <break time="0.8s" /> By most 8 year old human children. <break time="0.8s" /> But by hardly any 4 year olds. <break time="0.8s" /> Rationally it seems that one solves this problem. <break time="0.8s" /> By imagining various things one might do with the available materials. <break time="0.8s" /> Until one hits on the correct solution. <break time="0.8s" /> We do not know. <break time="0.8s" /> That the animals in question. <break time="0.8s" /> Achieve their insights in the same way, of course. <break time="0.8s" /> But the simplest hypothesis is that they do.
